title: DeviceChain — Persistence and state
description: Operations board for storage: events written to the event store, the live device state built from them, the background jobs that repair and rebuild history, the databases (the shared relational database and this instance's event store) with their connections, replication, write-ahead log shipping, backups and disks, and the progress of tenant removals. The relational database is shared by every instance in the cluster, so its panels show cluster-wide load. Not shown because the platform does not export it: the data-retention and compression reconciler, and the health of the backup object store itself (only its disk space is shown). Each instance gets its own copy of this board, scoped to it; there is no instance picker.

list.name: namespace
list.label: Instance
list.description: The instance this board reads. Empty on purpose: the chart's templates/grafana-dashboard.yaml replaces this entry with a hidden constant naming the instance it installs, so every namespace="$namespace" selector reads that instance's series and no other. There is no instance picker: each instance ships its own copy of this board, in its own Grafana folder.

list.name: instance
list.label: Instance ID
list.description: The instance ID, used to select this instance's alerts. Empty on purpose: the chart's templates/grafana-dashboard.yaml replaces this entry with a hidden constant holding the ID of the instance it installs.

panels.title: Firing alerts
panels.description: Alerts firing right now for this instance that concern the databases, their backups and disks, live device state and tenant removal. An empty table means none are firing. Alerts come from the instance's Prometheus rules, so the table stays empty if those rules are not installed.

panels.title: Events stored per second
panels.description: Events written to the event store. Zero while devices are sending means storage has stopped: check that event-management is running, then look at the waiting-work panel below and the database panels further down.

panels.title: Events not stored (selected range)
panels.description: Events that were not written. Failed ones were moved to the dead-letter store, dropped ones were discarded, and invalid ones were malformed and thrown away. Healthy is 0. When it is not, read the event-management log for the reason and check database health below.

panels.title: Events being retried per second
panels.description: Writes that failed for a temporary reason and were handed back to be tried again. A short burst is normal during a database failover. A sustained rate means the database is slow or refusing writes: see the database panels below.

panels.title: Writes in progress
panels.description: Events being written at this moment. A high number that stays high while the stored rate is low means writes are slow.

panels.title: Time to store one event (95th percentile)
panels.description: 95 out of 100 events are stored faster than this. Rising means the database is struggling: check connections, disk and long transactions below.

panels.title: Event results
panels.description: What happened to each event the store handled, per second. ok is stored. retry is handed back for another try. failed went to dead letters, dropped was discarded, invalid was malformed, and erased belongs to a tenant that has been deleted and was refused on purpose. Anything other than ok and a little retry deserves a look.

panels.title: Time to store one event
panels.description: How long it takes to store one event, by percentile. A rising 99th percentile with a steady median means a few slow writes, often a lock or a long transaction. Both rising together means the whole database is slow.

panels.title: Events per database transaction
panels.description: How many events are written together in one transaction. Larger batches mean the store is batching to keep up under load; batches of 1 mean there is little backlog to batch.

panels.title: Batches written again one by one
panels.description: Transactions that did not commit, after which their events were written again individually. An occasional one is harmless. A steady rate slows storing down and points at database contention or one bad event in the batches.

panels.title: Events waiting to be stored
panels.description: Messages queued for event-management that it has not finished handling. Growing while the stored rate is flat means storage cannot keep up. A queue that grows to its limit makes upstream services refuse new events, so act before that: see the database panels below. While the reading service is down this shows the message broker's own count.

targets.expr: max by (durable) ({__name__=~"devicechain_[a-z0-9]+_jetstream_consumer_pending_messages", namespace="$namespace", durable=~".+_event-management_.+"}) or max by (durable) (label_replace(nats_consumer_num_pending{namespace="$namespace", stream_name=~"${instance}_.+", consumer_name=~".+_event-management_.+"}, "durable", "$1", "consumer_name", "(.+)"))

panels.title: State updates per second
panels.description: Events merged into each device's live last-known state. Zero while events are being stored means the state service has stopped or fallen behind: see the waiting-work panel below.

panels.title: State updates lost (selected range)
panels.description: State updates that were dropped, failed or malformed. Dropped ones are discarded without a record, so a device's live state can be stale until its next event. Healthy is 0. Check the device-state log for the reason, and database health below.

panels.title: State updates being retried per second
panels.description: State updates that failed for a temporary reason and were handed back. A short burst is normal during a database failover; a sustained rate means the database is slow or refusing writes.

panels.title: State updates in progress
panels.description: State updates being merged at this moment.

panels.title: Time to update one state (95th percentile)
panels.description: 95 out of 100 state updates finish faster than this. Rising means the database is struggling, or many events are updating the same devices at once.

panels.title: State update results
panels.description: What happened to each state update, per second. ok is merged. retry is handed back for another try. failed went to dead letters, dropped was discarded, invalid was malformed, and erased belongs to a deleted tenant and was refused on purpose.

panels.title: Time to update one state
panels.description: How long it takes to merge one event into a device's state, by percentile. A rising 99th percentile with a steady median usually means contention on a few busy devices.

panels.title: Events per state transaction
panels.description: How many events are merged together in one transaction. Larger batches mean the service is batching to keep up; batches of 1 mean there is little backlog.

panels.title: Retried and repeated writes
panels.description: Batches that did not commit and were merged again, and single writes the database aborted as a deadlock or serialization conflict and that were run again. A steady rate means many events are touching the same devices at once. It slows the projection down but loses nothing.

targets.legendFormat: writes run again after a conflict

panels.title: Updates waiting to be applied
panels.description: Messages queued for device-state that it has not finished handling. Growing while the update rate is flat means live state is falling behind the event store.

panels.title: Time since the last inactivity check
panels.description: How long since the check that marks silent devices as inactive last finished its work. It should stay within a few of its intervals; a number that keeps climbing means the check has stopped and devices will not be marked inactive. Shows nothing until the first check completes.

panels.title: Background jobs in the event store
Time since the last history repair
panels.description: How long since the sweep that reconciles device history last finished its work. A number that keeps climbing means the sweep has stopped. Shows nothing until the first pass completes.

panels.title: History repair passes
panels.description: Passes of the history repair sweep per second, by outcome. A growing share of anything other than a clean pass means the sweep is failing: read the event-management log.

panels.title: Age of the oldest calculated-metric rebuild
panels.description: How long the oldest still-running rebuild of calculated-metric history has been going. Rebuilds run after a calculation changes. A job that stays here for hours is stuck or very large: check the rebuild panels beside this one.

panels.title: Calculated-metric rebuilds finished
panels.description: Rebuilds of calculated-metric history that finished, per second, by how they ended. Anything that ends in failure needs the event-management log.

panels.title: Rows written by rebuilds
panels.description: Calculated values written back to the event store by rebuilds, and the raw samples read to produce them, per second. Zero is normal when no rebuild is running.

panels.title: Work skipped by rebuilds
panels.description: Items a rebuild skipped, per second, by reason, and time windows it skipped, by cause. Skips are deliberate (for example data already past its retention), but a sudden rise means a rebuild is covering less than expected.

panels.title: Time to refresh the rollups
panels.description: How long a rebuild takes to refresh the stored summaries of telemetry (95th percentile). Slow refreshes hold up the end of a rebuild; collisions are shown in the panel beside it.

panels.title: Rollup refresh collisions
panels.description: Times a rollup refresh collided with another and had to be repeated. A few are normal; a steady rate stretches rebuilds out.

panels.title: Databases (the shared relational database and this instance's event store)
Database server
panels.description: Whether each database server answers its health check. Down means the database cannot be reached: services that depend on it will fail. Check the database pods in the database namespace.

panels.title: Cluster state
panels.description: Whether the database operator considers each database cluster ready. Not ready for more than a few minutes means a failover or restart that has not finished, or the operator cannot reconcile the cluster.

panels.title: Standbys streaming
panels.description: Standby copies currently receiving changes from each primary. Fewer than configured means a standby is down or has fallen out of sync, and a failover would have fewer places to go.

panels.title: Deadlocks (selected range)
panels.description: Times the database aborted a transaction to break a deadlock. A few are tolerable and retried; a steady stream means writers are fighting over the same rows.

panels.title: Connections in use
panels.description: Share of each database server's connection limit that is in use. Near 100 percent means new connections are refused and services stall: look for a service holding too many connections, or raise the limit.

targets.expr: sum by (namespace, pod) (cnpg_backends_total{namespace=~"@dbnamespace@|$namespace"}) / on (namespace, pod) max by (namespace, pod) (cnpg_pg_settings_setting{namespace=~"@dbnamespace@|$namespace", name="max_connections"})

panels.title: Longest open transaction
panels.description: Age of the longest transaction still open on each database server. A transaction held open for minutes blocks cleanup and can block other writers. Find and stop what is holding it.

panels.title: Commits and rollbacks
panels.description: Transactions committed and rolled back per second, across all databases. A rising rollback share means writers are failing and retrying.

panels.title: Database size
panels.description: On-disk size of each database. Steady growth is expected; a sudden jump means a bulk load or a retention policy that stopped removing old data. Compare with the disk panels below.

panels.title: Standby delay
panels.description: How far each standby is behind its primary, in seconds. A delay that keeps growing means the standby cannot keep up or has lost its connection, and a failover would lose that much recent data.

panels.title: Age of the oldest unfrozen transaction
panels.description: How close each database is to transaction-number wraparound. The database must clean up before about 2 billion; above 1 billion, check that automatic vacuum is running and is not blocked by a long transaction.

panels.title: Which pod is the primary
panels.description: Each database pod appears at 1 while it holds the primary role and has no line otherwise. A planned switchover or a failover shows as one pod's line ending and another's starting. Database pods are named for their database, so the lines of the two databases are told apart by name.

panels.title: Primary changes (selected range)
panels.description: How many times a database changed primary in the selected range, counted from the pods that switched between primary and standby. A planned switchover or a failover counts once. More than expected means the primary is being lost: look at the database pods' events and the node they ran on.

panels.title: Log segments waiting to ship
panels.description: Write-ahead log segments the database has finished but not yet copied to the backup destination, on the busiest server. Above about 30 for several minutes means shipping is stuck and the server's disk will fill with log files.

panels.title: Log shipping failures (selected range)
panels.description: Times copying a log segment to the backup destination failed. Healthy is 0. Failures stop point-in-time recovery from advancing: check the backup destination and its credentials.

panels.title: Time since last log segment shipped
panels.description: Seconds since a log segment was last copied to the backup destination, on the server with the longest gap. A server that has never shipped one shows -1. Long gaps on a busy database mean shipping is stuck.

panels.title: Age of the newest base backup
panels.description: How long ago the newest full backup finished, for the cluster with the oldest one. Compare against your backup schedule: more than 36 hours is a missed daily backup, and more than about 8 days is a missed weekly one. Shows nothing if backups are not enabled.

panels.title: Log segments shipped per second
panels.description: Write-ahead log segments copied to the backup destination, and failed attempts, per second. The shipped line should follow database write activity; any failed line above zero needs attention.

panels.title: Log segments waiting to ship over time
panels.description: Segments queued to be copied to the backup destination, per server. A line that climbs and never drops means shipping is stuck.

panels.title: Fullest database disk
panels.description: Used share of the fullest database volume, including log volumes. Above 75 percent is a warning and above 85 percent is urgent: a full database disk stops all writes. Expand the volume or reduce retention.

panels.title: Fullest backup destination disk
panels.description: Used share of the backup object store volume. Above 85 percent is urgent: when it fills, log shipping and backups stop. Shows nothing if the object store is not on a volume this cluster monitors.

panels.title: Shortest time until the event store disk is full
panels.description: Based on the last 15 minutes of use, how long until the event store disk is full. Shows nothing while usage is flat or falling. Under 24 hours means act now.

panels.title: Database disk free space
panels.description: Free share of each database volume (data and log volumes). The database stops accepting writes when a volume is full; the alerts fire at 25 percent free, 15 percent free, and on a fast-falling trend.

panels.title: Database disk used
panels.description: Bytes used on each database volume. Compare slopes: the event store grows with telemetry volume, the relational database with configuration and audit history.

panels.title: Backup destination free space
panels.description: Free share of the backup object store volume. Shows nothing if the object store does not use a volume this cluster monitors.

panels.title: Largest history tables
panels.description: On-disk size of the tables that only ever grow (such as the audit trail), as reported by each service, ten largest. Nothing prunes these, so rising is expected: use this to plan disk, not as a fault. Taken as the maximum across replicas, never a sum.

panels.title: History table row counts
panels.description: Estimated rows in the same tables, from the database's planner statistics, so approximate. Rises with activity; a sudden steep climb points at a noisy writer.

panels.title: Deletions in progress
panels.description: Tenant deletions that are open right now. Reported by the one user-management replica that runs removals, so a standby reads zero. Each should finish within a few minutes plus the configured hold.

panels.title: Oldest open deletion
panels.description: Age of the longest-open tenant deletion. If this passes twice the configured hold the removal is stuck and the tenant's data has not been erased: see which store is holding it in the panel below.

panels.title: Deletions completed (selected range)
panels.description: Tenant deletions that fully finished in the selected time range: every store clean and the tenant name released.

panels.title: Removal failures (selected range)
panels.description: Times the removal coordinator could not carry a deletion through a pass. The deletion is retried, so an occasional failure is fine; repeated failures mean it is stuck. The user-management log names the tenant and the step.

panels.title: Stores holding up a deletion
panels.description: Open deletions each storage system is holding back. deferred means the store still reports data present or arriving; error means it could not answer. A store stuck on deferred is either retaining data on purpose or still being written to for the deleted tenant.

panels.title: Rows erased per second
panels.description: Rows, objects, messages or keys erased per second for deleted tenants, by store. Use it to tell a slow store from a stuck one: slow still shows progress.

panels.title: Time for one erase call
panels.description: How long each store took to answer one erase request (95th percentile). A store that takes minutes per call is the likely bottleneck of a slow deletion.
